name: Meclofenoxate (Centrophenoxine)

lead: Meclofenoxate (centrophenoxine) is an ester of dimethylaminoethanol (DMAE) and 4-chlorophenoxyacetic acid. It is sold as a prescription drug in Japan and some European countries, under names such as Lucidril, and as a supplement in the US.

Its "anti-aging" reputation rests on lipofuscin (age pigment) findings in the brain and a reported 26.5 percent lifespan increase in mice. A 1977 study reported improved memory-test performance in elderly patients. No studies have tested it on skin.

paras: It is classed as a cholinergic nootropic; animal studies report changes in brain monoamines and protection in cerebral ischemia models.

Rare effects include insomnia, dizziness, restlessness, tremor, depression, nausea and headache, which Wikipedia says may reflect overdose. Brazil lists it as a controlled substance (2023) and it is not FDA-approved.

lead: Meclofenoxate, also called centrophenoxine, is an ester of dimethylethanolamine (DMAE) and 4-chlorophenoxyacetic acid.[1] It is sold as a prescription drug in Japan and some European countries including Germany, Hungary and Austria, and as a supplement elsewhere.[1]

Published human research is mostly from the 1970s and 1980s and animal work. A claim of a 26.5 percent lifespan increase in mice and a 1977 elderly memory study are the basis of its "anti-aging" reputation.[1]

paras: Wikipedia lists it only as cholinergic.[1] A rat study compared its effects on brain noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin with other nootropics[2], and a mouse study followed its metabolism to DMAE.[3] Grokipedia (AI-generated) describes lipofuscin reduction and cerebral ischemia protection in animal models.[4][5]

A 1977 study by Marcer and Hopkins in Age and Ageing reported improved performance on some memory tests in elderly patients.[6] A 1978 study measured lipofuscin pigment in senile dementia patients and noted prior reports of mental improvement with meclofenoxate.[7] A registered trial combines it with coenzyme Q10 in hepatic encephalopathy.[8] No studies of meclofenoxate on skin aging have been found.

Rare effects are insomnia, dizziness, restlessness, tremor, depression, nausea, muscle tension and headache.[1] It is generally prescription-only, Brazil classified it as controlled in 2023 and it is unapproved in the US.[1] A 2023 review discusses it among unauthorized ingredients in nootropic supplements.[9]
